summary: Defines a simple string encoding of Presentation Addresses for environments where a text form is useful. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1278 gives OSI presentation addresses a written form. A presentation address names another application on the network, and this syntax writes one as ordinary text, so a system manager can read it, type it and compare two of them.

subtitle: A plain-text way to write down an OSI presentation address so a person can read and type it.

tldr.problem: An OSI presentation address is normally kept as an ASN.1 structure in the OSI Directory, which people cannot easily read, type or print.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1278 defines a string syntax. Up to three selectors are written before slashes, and one or more network addresses follow, joined with underscores. Selectors come in four encodings and network addresses in several forms.
tldr.outcome: The format is for showing an address to system managers, not for storing one, and macros give short names for recurring addresses. The memo is Informational and says nothing about security.

today: RFC 1278 is an Informational memo, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a display format for OSI presentation addresses, written for the ISODE and THORN projects that the memo names.

sections.title: Why a String Form
sections.content:
OSI Application Entities use presentation addresses to address other Application Entities, and the model for this comes from the ISO reference on naming and addressing. Logically, a presentation address consists of a presentation selector, a session selector, a transport selector and a set of network addresses. The selectors are all octet strings, but they often have IA5 character representations. The format of the network addresses is defined in the ISO network services reference.

The OSI Directory stores these addresses using an ASN.1 representation. RFC 1278 adds a string encoding for the many contexts that need one. The memo says it is for display to human users, typically system managers rather than end users, and that its use is recommended whenever this needs to be done. It is not intended for internal storage.

The syntax was originally published as a University College London research note and was agreed as a unified syntax for the THORN and ISODE projects. It is used throughout ISODE.
sections.plainLanguage: An address is normally stored as a bundle of structured data. This memo gives it a written form that a person can read and type without special software.

sections.title: What the Format Must Do
sections.content:
The format must be able to specify any legal value. It must also deal with selectors in four encodings: IA5, decimal digits encoded as IA5, a number encoded as a 16 bit unsigned integer (US GOSIP), and general hexadecimal. Decimal digits as IA5 is the most common syntax in Europe, because X.400(84) requires it, and the memo says it should receive a straightforward encoding. The US GOSIP number is mapped onto two octets, with the first octet being the high order byte of the integer.

The format should be clean in the common case, where a presentation address holds network addresses and no selectors. It should give special encodings for the ad hoc encoding proposed in RFC 1277 for X.25(80) networks and TCP/IP networks, should be extensible for additional forms, and should provide a reasonably compact representation.
sections.plainLanguage: The text format has to be able to write every possible address, keep the usual simple case tidy, and leave room for new kinds of address later.

sections.title: The String Syntax
sections.content:
A presentation address string has up to three selectors, each followed by a slash, and then a list of network addresses. The selectors appear in the order presentation, session and transport. The leading ones may be left out: a transport selector on its own is allowed, but a session selector needs a transport selector as well. Several network addresses are joined with an underscore.

A selector is written in one of four ways: a quoted IA5 string, where characters outside that string are written in hex; a hash sign followed by decimal digits, which is US GOSIP; a hex string in single quotes followed by H; or nothing at all, meaning empty but present.

A network address has three forms. NS+ followed by a dotted decimal or hex string is the compact concrete binary form. The user oriented form is an afi, an idi and an optional dsp, where the afi is one of X121, DCC, TELEX, PSTN, ISDN, ICD or LOCAL. The third form is a digit string plus a hex string, for compatibility with ISO 8348. The dsp part can be abstract decimal (d), abstract binary (x), local IA5 (l), or one of the special forms RFC-1006, X.25(80), ECMA-117-Binary and ECMA-117-Decimal.

The RFC-1006 form takes either a dotted decimal IP address or a DNS domain name. The domain name is there for ease of entry. If the domain name maps onto multiple IP addresses, then multiple network addresses should be generated. When mapping from an encoded address to string form, the IP address form should always be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is written left to right: optional labels for the program, then the machine address itself. Several machine addresses can be joined with an underscore when one place has more than one.

sections.title: Encoding and Example Addresses
sections.content:
Section 4 explains what the two notations mean. In the NS notation, the concrete binary form of a network address is given. Otherwise the string notation provides a mechanism for representing the abstract syntax of a network address, and that abstract syntax must be encoded according to Addendum 2 of ISO 8348.

Figure 1 gives the grammar, and four example addresses follow it. The first has one transport selector and two network addresses. The second has all three selectors written in US GOSIP form, followed by an X.121 address. The third mixes a hex selector with a TELEX address that carries an X.25(80) part. The fourth is a bare RFC 1006 address with no selectors at all, which shows the clean common case the requirements ask for.
sections.plainLanguage: These are four sample addresses, from a simple one with no labels to a longer one with every part filled in.

sections.title: Macros for Common Addresses
sections.content:
Some addresses recur often enough to deserve a short name, and the memo calls these macros. If a network address can be parsed as a string, then =, then anything else, the leading string is taken as a macro and substituted for. Substitution may be applied recursively. When a network address is presented to people, the longest available substitution should be used.

The example in the memo is a two-level table. UK.AC stands for DCC+826+d110000, and Leeds stands for UK.AC=120 with more characters. Under that scheme, Leeds=22 expands to DCC+826+d11000012022.

The memo warns that no macro should ever be relied on, but it suggests four as standard: Int-X25(80), Janet-X25(80), Internet-RFC-1006 and IXI. Each expands to a TELEX prefix followed by an X.25(80) or RFC-1006 part.
sections.plainLanguage: A macro is a nickname for a long piece of an address. The computer swaps the nickname for the full text when it needs the full text.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states only that security considerations are not discussed. The string format is a notation for people to read, so it defines no protections of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss safety. It is only about how to write an address down.
